title: Typing | Fun Facts: Did You Know?
description: This course is for the continued development of typing skills for students who have already mastered touch typing basics. Students will type and discover fun facts relating to famous firsts, world records. unsolved mysteries and more in 200 lessons.

lessons.name: Number Fun Introduction
lessons.text1: There are infinite numbers! You can keep counting forever, and you'll never run out of numbers. For now, let's just practice your typing skills with some number fun!

lessons.name: 24 Hours
lessons.text1: There are 24 hours in a day, which is the same as 1,440 minutes or 86,400 seconds!

lessons.name: Odd Numbers
lessons.text1: Adding an even number to an odd number always gives an odd number. Try it! (4 + 5 = 9)

lessons.name: Repeating
lessons.text1: Multiply 37 by 3, 6, or 9. The results (111, 222, 333, etc.) are always repeating digits!

lessons.name: Palindromes
lessons.text1: Numbers like 121, 343, and 12321 read the same forward and backward. They're called palindromes!

lessons.name: Zero
lessons.text1: No matter how big a number is, multiplying it by zero always makes it zero. It's like a magical eraser!

lessons.name: Opposite
lessons.text1: The opposite sides on a die always add up to 7. The possible combinations include 1 + 6, 2 + 5, and 3 + 4.

lessons.name: Alphabetical
lessons.text1: 40 is the only number spelled in alphabetical order. When you write it out ("forty"), the letters are in order.

lessons.name: E
lessons.text1: Every odd number has an "e" in its name when written in English. One, three, five, seven, nine, eleven, etc. Should we keep going?

lessons.name: Number Fun Game 1
lessons.text1: minutes odd even multiply digits zero combinations forty

lessons.name: Divisible
lessons.text1: Try out this multiplication trick! If you multiply any number by 9, and then add the digits, the result will always be divisible by 9. Let's try it now!

lessons.name: Earth
lessons.text1: How heavy is the planet Earth? Scientists state that our planet weighs about 6,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 kilograms. That's 6 followed by 21 zeros!

lessons.name: Calendar
lessons.text1:
A deck of cards is like a calendar: 52 cards = 52 weeks in a year. 4 suits = 4 seasons. 12 face cards = 12 months.
Add the values of all cards (with Jack = 11, Queen = 12, King = 13), and you get 365!

lessons.name: Age
lessons.text1: Did you know that if you add your age to the year you were born, it will always equal the current year? Go ahead and try this! Now, ask someone older than you to see if it works again!

lessons.name: Multiply
lessons.text1: Multiplying large numbers is easier than it seems. Want to multiply 25 x 16 in your head? Split it up! 25 x 10 = 250. Then 25 x 6 = 150. Now, add them together: 250 + 150 = 400! Try it with another equation!

lessons.name: Months
lessons.text1: When babies are born, we measure their age in months. After you turn 12 months (or 1 year old), age is measured in years. Ever wonder how many months old you are? Multiply your age by 12 to find out!

lessons.name: Fingers
lessons.text1: To multiply any number by 9, hold up both hands. Lower the finger corresponding to the number you're multiplying. For example, for 4 x 9, lower your fourth finger. Count the fingers before it (3) and after it (6). The answer is 36!

lessons.name: Pi Day
lessons.text1: "Pi Day" is celebrated on March 14th because Pi's first three digits are 3.14. Pi is the mathematical constant that represents the ratio of a circle's circumference to its diameter. In 2019, Google calculated Pi to 31.4 trillion digits after the decimal point. In 2022, they calculated it to 100 trillion digits!

lessons.text1: divisible Earth scientist calendar equal age equation babies measure months fingers Pi circumference

lessons.name: Word Fun Introduction
lessons.text1: You may not know it, but words often have a fun origin or interesting story tied to them. Learn about words while improving your typing speed and accuracy!

lessons.name: Longest Word
lessons.text1: Can you type one of the longest words in the English language? Give it a try now: floccinaucinihilipilification!

lessons.name: Worthless
lessons.text1: Floccinaucinihilipilification combines several Latin word stems. It means the act of describing something as worthless. It is one letter longer than antidisestablishmentarianism!

lessons.name: Longest Name
lessons.text1: The longest name in any English-speaking country is 85 characters long! It's the name of a hill located in New Zealand. Want to try typing it? Okay, let's go, but be careful!

lessons.name: Taumata
lessons.text1:
Taumatawhakatangihangakoauauotamateapokaiwhenuakitanatahu.
Great job! That was a challenging word! Locals call this hill "Taumata" for short.

lessons.name: QWERTY
lessons.text1: Did you know you can type some really long words using just the left side of a QWERTY keyboard? Let's try it now: stewardesses, aftercataracts, devertebrated. Good job! Let's keep going!

lessons.name: Right Side
lessons.text1: If you thought that was a challenge, did you know you can also type some words with just the right side of the keyboard? Like phyllophyllin! How did you do with trying this word? Did you type all of the letters correctly?

lessons.name: Top Row
lessons.text1: There are even words you can type with just the top row: teetertotter and rupturewort! Teetertotter is another word for a child's seesaw, and rupturewort is a type of plant. Can you see any other words you can type using only the top row?

lessons.name: Shortest Word
lessons.text1: The shortest word in the English language is the article "a." "I" and "o" are also one letter long. The word "a" is a monophthong, or one vowel sound in a single syllable, while "I" and "o" are dipthongs, or two vowel sounds in a single syllable.

lessons.name: Word Fun Game 1
lessons.text1: longest stems Latin character Taumata left right top shortest English syllable

lessons.name: Vowels
lessons.text1: Here's an interesting word fact about numbers! If you spell out every number from 0 to 999, you will find every vowel except for "a." You have to count to one thousand to find an a!

lessons.name: Oology
lessons.text1: The study of bird eggs is called oology. It's the shortest scientific word ending in -ology. It's only 6 letters long! Seven letter words ending in -ology include geology, noology, orology, zoology, and enology.

lessons.name: New Words
lessons.text1: Can you believe that approximately one new word is added to the English language every two hours and around 4,000 new words are added to the English dictionary every year? That's a lot of new words getting created all the time. Who knows, maybe you'll think of a new word!

lessons.name: Phobia
lessons.text1: A phobia is an irrational or abnormal fear of something. "Phobia" can be used as a suffix to create terms for fears. For example, pogonophobia is a fear of beards. Zoophobia is a fear of animals, and chronophobia is a fear of time. Can you guess what a fear of phobias is called? Phobophobia!

lessons.name: Shakespeare
lessons.text1: Shakespeare's plays contain the first recorded use of over 1,700 words! He invented many of these words himself by combining existing words, turning them into verbs, or adding new prefixes and suffixes. These words include: bedroom, eyeball, gossip, manager, kissing, hurry, traditional, and zany!

lessons.name: Tongue Twister
lessons.text1:
Do you like tongue twisters? Try this one: sixth sick sheik's sixth sheep's sick. Guinness World Records once said this was the hardest tongue twister in the English language.
Another one of the hardest tongue twisters is: pad kid poured curd pulled cod. Try saying that out loud now. How did you do?

lessons.name: Singular
lessons.text1: A single strand of spaghetti is called a "spaghetto," while a group of spaghetti strands is called "spaghetti." Such is also the case for other pastas! "Gnocco" is the singular of "gnocchi," and "raviolo" is the singular of "ravioli." This naming convention is a common feature of the Italian language.

lessons.name: Niche
lessons.text1: The word "niche" is often used to describe a skill a person has, but do you know how to pronounce it? Do you say "nich," rhyming with "itch," or "neesh," rhyming with "sheesh"? Well, guess what? Both are correct! Whether you say it one way or the other, you're right. Both pronunciations are widely accepted.

lessons.name: Common
lessons.text1: Can you guess the most commonly used word in English? Take a moment before reading the answer! Got it? It's "the," the most frequently used English word. In second place is the verb "be" (and its forms), followed by the conjunction "and." The rest of the top 10 includes "a," "of," "to," "in," "I," "you," and "it."

lessons.name: Sports Trivia Introduction
lessons.text1: There is more to sports than just how to play the games. Let's practice your typing skills while you learn some interesting facts about sports!

lessons.name: Pucks
lessons.text1: Ice hockey pucks are frozen before a game to make them slide more smoothly on the ice and to reduce bouncing.

lessons.name: Lightning Strike
lessons.text1: In 1919, Cleveland Indians pitcher Ray Caldwell was struck by lightning in the middle of the 9th inning. He kept playing!

lessons.name: Super Bowl MVP
lessons.text1: Joe Montana was the first player to win Super Bowl MVP three times, achieving this honor in Super Bowls XVI, XIX, and XXIV.

lessons.name: Tennis Balls
lessons.text1: Tennis balls used to be white! The bright yellow color we see today was introduced in 1972 so they could be seen more easily on television.

lessons.name: FIFA
lessons.text1: The FIFA World Cup is the most watched sporting event in the world. Billions of people from all over the world tune in to this event every four years.

lessons.name: Moon
lessons.text1: Golf is one of only two sports ever played on the moon. In 1971, Alan Shepard hit a ball with a six-iron while on the moon as part of the Apollo 14 mission.

lessons.name: Home Run
lessons.text1: One of Babe Ruth's nicknames was "The Sultan of Swat." The baseball legend earned this nickname because he hit so many home runs, swatting the ball out of the park.

lessons.name: Volleyball
lessons.text1: When volleyball was invented in 1895, it was first called "Mintonette." The name was later changed to volleyball because the ball is "volleyed" back and forth over the net.

lessons.name: Sports Trivia Game 1
lessons.text1: hockey baseball soccer golf volleyball tennis lightning puck pitcher

lessons.name: Extreme Sports
lessons.text1: The term "extreme sports" became popular in the 1990s, encompassing activities like skateboarding, snowboarding, and BMX biking. There are now about 100 extreme sports for thrill seekers!

lessons.name: Baseball Stitches
lessons.text1: There are 108 stitches on a regulation baseball. That stitching plays a significant role in the trajectory of a thrown baseball due to the drag caused by the interaction between the stitching and the air.

lessons.name: Canceled Games
lessons.text1: The Olympic Games have only been canceled three times. These cancellations were due to World Wars: in 1916 (World War I) and 1940 and 1944 (World War II). The 2020 pandemic postponed the games by 1 year.

lessons.name: Polygons
lessons.text1: The standard soccer ball is stitched or glued together from 32 polygons. 12 of them are five-sided pentagons, and 20 are six-sided hexagons. They are arranged in such a way that every pentagon is surrounded by hexagons.

lessons.name: Olympic Rings
lessons.text1: The Olympic Rings symbol represents the union of the five continents and their athletes that perform at the Olympics. The continents are the Americas (once considered one continent), Europe, Asia, Africa, and Oceania.

lessons.name: 100-Meter Dash
lessons.text1: The 100-meter dash is a sprint race in track and field competitions. The men's world record is 9.58 seconds, set by Jamaica's Usain Bolt in 2009, while the women's world record is 10.49 seconds, set by American Florence Griffith-Joyner in 1988.

lessons.name: Hole-In-One
lessons.text1: According to the National Hole-In-One Registry, the odds of a professional golfer making a hole-in-one are about 1 in 3,000. Those are pretty slim chances! For amateur golfers, the odds are closer to 1 in 12,500. Can you guess the chance of making two holes-in-one in the same round? 1 in 67 million!

lessons.name: Basketball
lessons.text1: In December 1891, James Naismith, a physical education teacher, invented a new game called basketball to entertain the school's athletes in the winter season. He appointed captains of two nine-player teams, and they played this new game with a soccer ball and two fruit baskets tacked to either end of the gymnasium.

lessons.name: Mongol Derby
lessons.text1: The world's longest horse race is the Mongol Derby. It is an equestrian endurance race that extends 1,000 kilometers (620 miles) through the Mongolian Steppe and lasts 10 days. Only about half of the riders complete the race each year! The course recreates the horse messenger system developed by Genghis Khan in 1224.

lessons.name: Famous Firsts Introduction
lessons.text1: These "firsts" highlight achievements and milestones throughout history. Practice your typing skills while you learn some famous firsts!

lessons.name: First Computer
lessons.text1: The ENIAC was the first general-purpose computer, and it was huge! It took up an entire room.

lessons.name: Olympia
lessons.text1: The first Olympic Games were held in Olympia, Greece in 776 BCE, featuring only one event: a foot race.

lessons.name: Voting
lessons.text1: In 1893, New Zealand became the first country to grant women the right to vote in parliamentary elections.

lessons.name: Heart Transplant
lessons.text1: Dr. Christiaan Barnard performed the first successful heart transplant in South Africa on December 3, 1967.

lessons.name: Snow White
lessons.text1: The first full-length animated feature was Snow White and the Seven Dwarfs, which was released by Disney in 1937.

lessons.name: Despacito
lessons.text1: The first video to reach 1 billion views on YouTube was Luis Fonsi's "Despacito." This milestone was achieved in 2017.

lessons.name: Lindbergh
lessons.text1: Charles Lindbergh made the first solo nonstop flight across the Atlantic Ocean on May 20-21, 1927, flying from New York to Paris.

lessons.name: Amelia Earhart
lessons.text1: Amelia Earhart was the first woman to fly alone across the Atlantic Ocean. She was a pioneer in aviation and an inspiration to many.

lessons.name: Famous Firsts Game 1
lessons.text1: achievement milestone first successful pioneer inspiration changed forever Lindbergh win received

lessons.name: Mount Everest
lessons.text1: Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay were the first to reach the summit of Mount Everest on May 29, 1953. Mount Everest is 29,032 feet high!

lessons.name: The Wright Brothers
lessons.text1: The Wright brothers, Orville and Wilbur, were the first to fly an airplane. Their first flight lasted just 12 seconds, but it changed transportation forever.

lessons.name: First Email
lessons.text1: Ray Tomlinson sent the first email over the ARPANET in 1971. It was initially an experiment to see if he could get two computers to exchange a message. The message was "QWERTYUIOP"!

lessons.name: Marie Curie
lessons.text1: Marie Curie was the first woman to win a Nobel Prize. She received the award in Physics in 1903. She was a physicist and a chemist. She is known for her pioneering research into radioactivity.

lessons.name: Barack Obama
lessons.text1: Barack Obama was inaugurated as the first African-American president of the United States on January 20, 2009. His wife, Michelle Obama, also became the first African-American First Lady of the United States.

lessons.name: Apollo 11
lessons.text1: Neil Armstrong became the first person to walk on the Moon on July 20, 1969. This historic event took place during the Apollo 11 mission. He said the famous words: "That's one small step for man, one giant leap for mankind."

lessons.name: Supreme Court
lessons.text1: Sandra Day O'Connor was an American attorney, politician, and jurist who served as an associate justice of the Supreme Court of the United States from 1981 to 2006. Appointed by President Ronald Reagan in 1981, she was the first woman to serve on the U.S. Supreme Court.

lessons.name: Remote
lessons.text1: The first T.V. remote control, called the "Lazy Bones," was invented by Robert Adler in 1950. Before this invention, people would have to get up and manually change the channel or volume on the T.V.! Can you imagine having to do that each time you wanted to change the channel or the volume?

lessons.name: Telephone Directory
lessons.text1: The first telephone directory was published in 1878, just two years after Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone. The directory was just one page long and only included 50 names and addresses! Later that year, the same company released the first phone book, which contained 391 names and addresses.

lessons.name: Unsolved Mysteries Introduction
lessons.text1: Throughout history, there have been many mysterious events. Let's practice your typing skills while you learn about some unsolved mysteries!

lessons.name: Bermuda Triangle
lessons.text1: The Bermuda Triangle in the Atlantic Ocean is famous for the unexplained disappearance of ships and airplanes, but no definite answers are known about what causes this.

lessons.name: Alcatraz
lessons.text1: Three men escaped from the island prison of Alcatraz, off the coast of San Francisco, in 1960. They made it to their raft but whether they made it to shore is unknown.

lessons.name: Kryptos
lessons.text1: On the grounds of the Central Intelligence Agency stands "Kryptos," a sculpture made of four coded messages. Three of the messages have been decoded, but the fourth remains a mystery.

lessons.name: Atlantis
lessons.text1: The Greek philosopher Plato wrote about the doomed island of Atlantis that ruled the Western part of the world before becoming lost beneath the sea. This supposed civilization has never been found.

lessons.name: Flying Dutchman
lessons.text1: The Flying Dutchman is a legendary ghost ship that is said to appear to sailors. According to legend, the ship is doomed to sail the seas forever, and seeing it is a bad omen.

lessons.name: Crop Circles
lessons.text1: Crop circles are large, intricate patterns that appear in fields of crops, often overnight. Some people think they are made by aliens, while others believe they are created by humans as a prank.

lessons.name: King Tut
lessons.text1: When archaeologists discovered the tomb of the Egyptian pharaoh King Tut in 1922, a legend of a curse began. Many of the people involved in the excavation later became ill or met mysterious fates.

lessons.name: Pyramids
lessons.text1: The ancient Egyptians built massive pyramids with enormous stone blocks. But how did they move such huge stones without modern tools? There are theories that ramps and levers were used, but the exact methods are still a mystery!

lessons.name: Unsolved Mysteries Game 1
lessons.text1: mysterious ships civilization disappeared ghost legendary appear unknown strange unsolved found

lessons.name: The Taos Hum
lessons.text1: In Taos, New Mexico, a mysterious low hum baffles locals. Only some hear it, often at night, causing stress and disrupted sleep. Despite theories like seismic activity or psychological causes, its true source remains unknown.

lessons.name: Apollo 12
lessons.text1: During the Apollo 12 mission, astronauts reported seeing strange footprints on the Moon that didn't belong to them. They found footprints where no one had walked before. Could there have been a mysterious visitor on the Moon before them?

lessons.name: Voynich Manuscript
lessons.text1: The Voynich Manuscript is an ancient book filled with strange, unreadable writing and mysterious drawings of plants, people, and animals that don't seem to exist. No one has been able to crack the code or understand what the book is about.

lessons.name: Bigfoot
lessons.text1: Many people believe that Bigfoot, a giant, hairy creature, roams the forests of North America. There are many sightings and blurry photos. People have claimed to see him or his footprints. But no one has been able to produce any solid proof.

lessons.name: Art Heist
lessons.text1: On March 18th, 1990, thirteen pieces of art worth hundreds of millions of dollars were stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston, MA. The case is still unsolved, and none of the pieces have been located yet. The Museum, the FBI, and the U.S. Attorney's office are still on the case!

lessons.name: Dance in France
lessons.text1: In 1518, dozens of people in France suddenly began dancing uncontrollably. It lasted for days! The people couldn't stop dancing. Some even collapsed from exhaustion. Historians are puzzled by what caused it. Some believe it was mass hysteria, while others think it might have been a mysterious illness.

lessons.name: Amelia Earhart
lessons.text1: Amelia Earhart was a famous pilot. She disappeared while flying over the Pacific Ocean in 1937. No one knows what actually happened to her. There are theories that her plane ran out of gas and crashed into the Pacific Ocean. Her plane has still not been recovered, so her disappearance remains a mystery.

lessons.name: Nazca Lines
lessons.text1: In the desert of Peru, there are gigantic drawings etched into the ground called the Nazca Lines. These drawings, called geoglyphs, depict animals, plants, and other shapes. What makes it mysterious is how these massive images were made thousands of years ago and why...especially since they can only be fully seen from the sky!

lessons.name: Mary Celeste
lessons.text1: The Mary Celeste was a ship found floating in the Atlantic Ocean in 1872, completely empty. The crew had disappeared, but all their belongings, including food and personal items, were still on board. The ship was in perfect condition, and there was no sign of a struggle. To this day, no one knows what happened to the people on board.

lessons.name: Fascinating Foods Introduction
lessons.text1: What's your favorite food? Whether it's ice cream, fries, strawberries, or something else, you'll learn tons of fun facts about amazing foods while you practice typing.

lessons.name: Purple Carrots
lessons.text1: Carrots were originally purple until the 17th century when Dutch breeders developed the orange variety.

lessons.name: Fries
lessons.text1: I'll have fries with that! Did you know that french fries aren't French? They were invented in Belgium, where they are typically served with mayonnaise.

lessons.name: Apples
lessons.text1: Apple bobbing, anyone? Did you know that apples float because they're 25% air? This makes them perfect for fun science experiments or bobbing for them in the fall.

lessons.name: Strawberries
lessons.text1: Strawberries are the only fruit that have seeds on the outside. In fact, this means strawberries aren't true berries. Each strawberry seed is thought to be its own fruit by botanists!

lessons.name: Space Potatoes
lessons.text1: Are you aware that potatoes were the first food grown in space, thanks to NASA and the University of Wisconsin? The next time you're eating a potato, look up at the sky and imagine them growing in space!

lessons.name: Cream Ice
lessons.text1: Ice cream used to be called "cream ice" in 17th-century England, and it was typically enjoyed by royalty across Western Europe. By 1660, however, a cafe selling ice cream opened so it could be enjoyed by all!

lessons.name: Fruits
lessons.text1: Hungry for a salad? Let's make it a fruit salad! Tomatoes, cucumbers, and avocados are actually fruits, not vegetables, according to botanists. This is because the flesh of the fruit surrounds the seeds.

lessons.name: Chickens
lessons.text1: There are more chickens than humans on Earth, with around 25 billion worldwide. As a global food staple, chickens far outnumber the human population, highlighting their importance in the global food supply chain.

lessons.name: Fascinating Foods Game 1
lessons.text1: carrots Belgium mayonnaise bobbing strawberries botanists space salad cream chickens

lessons.name: Milk
lessons.text1: Did you know it takes around 350 squirts from a cow's udder to make one gallon of milk? Dairy farmers work hard to provide this staple, with high-producing cows making several gallons daily!

lessons.name: Fancy Hot Dogs
lessons.text1: Did you know the world's priciest hot dog cost $169? Sold in Seattle, it featured fancy toppings like foie gras and shaved truffles. A true gourmet treat for hot dog fans with expensive taste!

lessons.name: Swiss Cheese
lessons.text1: Ever wonder why some cheeses, like Swiss, have holes? During fermentation, bacteria release gas, creating bubbles that form holes as the cheese matures. This process also adds to the cheese's distinctive flavor!

lessons.name: Longest Noodle
lessons.text1: The longest noodle ever made stretched an incredible 10,119 feet and 1.92 inches! Created in China by a team of chefs, this noodle could stretch across a football field multiple times. It's a record-breaking example of culinary creativity and teamwork!

lessons.name: Chef Hat
lessons.text1: A chef's hat isn't just for looks. It has 100 folds, symbolizing the 100 ways to cook an egg! From scrambled and fried to poached and baked, eggs are among the most versatile ingredients. The folds honor the mastery chefs must develop to perfect the many techniques used to prepare this staple food.

lessons.name: Sushi Roll
lessons.text1: The world's largest sushi roll was made in Boston, MA in 2022. The process, led by Nick DiGiovanni and Lynn Davis, took 3 hours. The roll was over 7 feet wide! DiGiovanni and Davis also achieved other records, such as Largest Chicken Nugget and Most Fast Food Restaurants Visited in 24 Hours.

lessons.name: Saffron
lessons.text1: The most expensive spice in the world is saffron, which is made from the dried stigmas of the Crocus sativus flower. It takes over 75,000 flowers to produce just one pound of saffron, and it must be harvested by hand, which is why it is so expensive. Despite its price, saffron has been used for thousands of years!

lessons.name: Fruit Stickers
lessons.text1: Have you ever been so hungry that you accidentally ate the sticker on your apple? No need to panic! The stickers are non-toxic and edible. While they aren't going to add any nutritional value to your snack, they won't harm you!

lessons.name: Carolina Reaper
lessons.text1: The world's hottest pepper is the Carolina Reaper, which was developed by Ed Currie in 2013. The pepper consistently measures between 1,400,000 to 2,200,000 Scoville heat units (SHU), surpassing the Trinidad Scorpion "Butch T" pepper. Eating a Carolina Reaper can cause intense pain and sweating. It can even cause hallucinations!

lessons.name: The Human Body Introduction
lessons.text1: Did you know your fingers work with your brain at lightning speed when you type? Discover other amazing facts about the human body while you practice your typing skills.

lessons.name: Nose and Ears
lessons.text1: Have you ever heard that your nose and ears never stop growing? Well, they certainly do appear to get bigger as you age, but not because they are growing! Gravity makes the cartilage in your ears and nose droop.

lessons.name: Teeth
lessons.text1: Human teeth are as strong as shark teeth! Just like humans, sharks have something called dentin inside their teeth, which is soft and flexible, surrounded by hard enamel. However, shark teeth are much sharper than human teeth!

lessons.name: Muscles
lessons.text1: Each physical action our bodies make, however simple, relies on one or more of our 650 muscles. For example, every step you take uses 200 different muscles in unison to lift the foot, propel it forward, and then rest it on the ground.

lessons.name: Skin
lessons.text1: Your skin is the largest organ in your body and acts as a barrier for the rest of your body. It accounts for 16 percent of your body weight! The largest internal organ by weight is the liver, and the longest internal organ is your small intestine!

lessons.name: Tongue Prints
lessons.text1: You might know that humans all have unique fingerprints. But did you know that we also have unique tongue prints? This discovery might shed some light on why different people have such different food preferences, since our tongue is where we taste food.

lessons.name: Bones
lessons.text1: Humans are born with about 300 bones, but some fuse together as we grow older. As a result, we only have around 206 left by the time we reach adulthood. The largest bone in our body, the femur, is also the strongest! In fact, the thigh bone is stronger than concrete.

lessons.name: Blush
lessons.text1: Feeling embarrassed? Whenever you blush, you are blushing on the inside of your body as well as the outside! The blood vessels in your body open wide when you are blushing, allowing more blood to flow through. This means that even your stomach lining blushes!

lessons.name: Sleep
lessons.text1: Sleep is essential! It accounts for about a quarter or a third of a person's life. Even though sleep appears to be a passive activity, your brain is sometimes more active while you're sleeping than when you're awake. As you sleep, your brain processes subconscious thoughts.

lessons.name: The Human Body Game 1
lessons.text1: gravity cartilage shark dentin muscles internal intestine fingerprints tongue femur blush subconscious

lessons.name: 1,000 Skins
lessons.text1: Your skin essentially replaces itself every month! It sheds 30,000 skin cells per minute. That means that you could have about 1,000 different skins during your lifetime!

lessons.name: Heart
lessons.text1: Your heart, about the size of your fist, works nonstop! It will beat over 2.5 billion times by age 70. It also pumps 2,000 gallons of blood daily. It's like having a superhero inside your chest!

lessons.name: Cartilage
lessons.text1: Did you know you're about 1 centimeter taller in the morning? As you move through the day, the soft cartilage between your bones gets squished, making you slightly shorter by bedtime! Cool, right?

lessons.name: Sweat
lessons.text1: Your body's sweat keeps you cool and protects you from overheating. Your body has 2 to 4 million sweat glands and most are located on your palms, feet, face, and armpits. This ensures you stay ready for anything...especially gym class!

lessons.name: Muscle Memory
lessons.text1: Your fingers are an amazing part of your body. Touch typing (what you're doing right now!) uses muscle memory to make your fingers move. Typing engages your brain's language, memory, and motor skills so that when you think of words, they'll flow almost seamlessly to your computer's screen!

lessons.name: Breathe
lessons.text1: It's impossible to breathe and swallow at the same time! That's because our bodies have a natural reflex called the "pharyngeal reflex." When we swallow, a flap of tissue called the epiglottis closes off the trachea, or windpipe, to make sure that food or liquid goes down the esophagus, or food pipe, instead.

lessons.name: Gas
lessons.text1: Can you guess how often the average person farts per day? The average range is between 10 and 20 times! Is that more than you thought? Each day, most people hold between 0.5 and 1.5 liters of gas in their intestines, which is released throughout the day. You create this gas by swallowing air and digesting food!

lessons.name: Twins
lessons.text1: Can you guess the longest length of time between two twins being born? 90 days! These twins were born in 1996 in Baltimore, Maryland. The first twin arrived three months prematurely on January 1st. The doctors were able to stop their mother's contractions, so the second twin wasn't born until March 30th!

lessons.name: Neurons
lessons.text1: How fast can you think? Each brain has about 100 billion neurons, or brain cells. These neurons communicate through electrochemical signals. In a mere second, one neuron can send up to 1,000 signals. This results in signals traveling from your brain to the rest of your body as fast as 200 miles per hour!

lessons.name: Mysterious Places Introduction
lessons.text1: Want to learn more about the most mysterious places in the world? Practice your typing skills while discovering interesting facts about these locations!

lessons.name: Area 51
lessons.text1: Area 51 is a top secret military base in Nevada where some believe the government is hiding proof of aliens and UFOs.

lessons.name: Lake Hillier
lessons.text1: Lake Hillier is bubblegum pink! While this may seem like something human-made, it's most likely caused by algae that appears in saltwater lakes.

lessons.name: Blood Falls
lessons.text1: In Antarctica, there is a waterfall that turns from clear to crimson mid-plunge. Scientists discovered that the water is full of tiny, iron-packed nanospheres that oxidize when they hit the air.

lessons.name: Loch Ness
lessons.text1: Loch Ness is a body of water in Scotland thought to be the home of a creature called "Nessie." Locals and tourists often visit to see if they can spot the Loch Ness Monster.

lessons.name: Marfa Lights
lessons.text1: In the town of Marfa, Texas, people have observed strange, orb-like lights in the distance at night for more than 100 years. Scientists have concluded that the strange lights are simply regular headlights being distorted by hot, desert air.

lessons.name: Crooked Forest
lessons.text1: The Crooked Forest of Poland is home to 400 trees that are mysteriously bent in the shape of a "J" at their base. Researchers aren't sure whether this happened because of a heavy snowfall, the Earth's gravitational pull, or something else.

lessons.name: Fiery Crater
lessons.text1: In Turkmenistan, there is a fiery crater known as "The Gates of Hell." It was accidentally made while scientists were drilling for oil. The ground where these scientists drilled collapsed, and the crater was set on fire on purpose to control the spread of any toxic gas. It's been burning since 1971!

lessons.name: The Lost Colony
lessons.text1: In 1587, a group of settlers established a colony on Roanoke Island, off present-day North Carolina. When their leader returned from England in 1590, he found the colony abandoned. The word "CROATOAN" was carved into a tree, but the settlers' fate has remained a mystery, sparking curiosity for centuries.

lessons.name: Patom Crater
lessons.text1: The Patom Crater is a strange rock formation that stands 130 feet high in a Siberian forest. The rock looks like a giant bird's nest, but scientists aren't sure whether this rock was shaped by a meteor strike, volcanic activity, or a gaseous impact.

lessons.name: Hessdalen
lessons.text1: Hessdalen, a small village in Norway, is known for having mysterious white, red, blue, green, and yellow lights that hover in the air. Floating over the valley near the village, these lights span about eight miles and can only be seen for about one hour a day.

lessons.name: Ain Dara Temple
lessons.text1: Syria is home to the Ain Dara Temple, where massive footprints were found carved into the stone floors. The footprints, more than three feet long, are thought to represent the steps of the temple's resident god. But the gods carved on the walls are all wearing shoes!

lessons.name: Sailing Stones
lessons.text1: In California's Death Valley, large rocks seem to move by themselves across the flat landscape, leaving long tracks behind them. These "sailing stones" confused scientists for many years, but the phenomenon is now thought to be caused by a combination of wind, water, and ice.

lessons.name: Eternal Flames Falls
lessons.text1: Eternal Flames Falls in New York is a strange waterfall that has a small grotto underneath where a flame burns. The flame is thought to be caused by the Earth's natural methane gas seeping through cracks in the ground, but this theory is still debated by researchers.

lessons.name: Clay Soldiers
lessons.text1: Qin Shi Huang, China's first emperor, has a tomb dating back to 200 BCE that was discovered by farmers in 1974. Once uncovered, the tomb was found to be guarded by more than 8,000 clay statues of army soldiers thought to be protecting this emperor in his afterlife.

lessons.name: Barsa-Kelmes
lessons.text1: Barsa-Kelmes in Kazakhstan used to be an island until the surrounding water dried up. It's nicknamed "the place of no return." Local legends tell of travelers who returned from Barsa-Kelmes after months or years, insisting they had only been there for days!

lessons.name: Cathedral Rock
lessons.text1: The Sedona red rock area of Arizona is home to Cathedral Rock. Many feel the area surrounding this rock contains healing powers where electromagnetic energies exist. Some say they've experienced a feeling of wellness here. Needless to say, this is a popular site for meditation.

lessons.name: Al Naslaa
lessons.text1: Saudi Arabia has a rock formation that continues to baffle scientists. Known as the Al Naslaa, this rock looks like it's been sliced in half. The cut in the middle is strangely straight and smooth. The two halves of the rock balance on natural pedestals coming up from the ground, making them look like they're floating.

lessons.name: World Records Introduction
lessons.text1: World records showcase extraordinary humans and incredible feats, inspiring awe and celebrating remarkable achievements. Let's learn about some world records while typing!

lessons.name: LEGO Tower
lessons.text1: Have you ever made a tower out of LEGOs? The world record for tallest LEGO tower is held by a team in Italy. Their LEGO tower reached a height of 114 feet!

lessons.name: Tallest Building
lessons.text1: The tallest building in the world is the Burj Khalifa in Dubai. It stands at 828 meters, or 2,717 feet, tall. That's a towering building!

lessons.name: Largest Bubble
lessons.text1: Have you ever blown a bubble? Chad Fell from the United States has the record for blowing the largest bubble. He blew a bubble measuring 20 inches in diameter.

lessons.name: Hot Wheels
lessons.text1: Do you think you could win the record for largest collection of Hot Wheels? Currently, Mike Zarnock from the USA holds the record with over 30,000 unique Hot Wheels cars.

lessons.name: Loudest Burp
lessons.text1: Excuse me! An Australian man named Neville Sharp set the record for the loudest burp at 112.4 decibels. That's louder than a trombone. He had been practicing for five years.

lessons.name: Loudest Burp 2
lessons.text1: What about loudest burp by a woman? The record for the loudest burp by a woman is held by Elisa Cagnoni, who recorded 107.0 decibels in Reggiolo, Italy, on June 16th, 2009.

lessons.name: Oldest Person
lessons.text1: Jeanne Louise Calment of France holds the record for the oldest person. She lived to be 122 years and 164 days old from 1875 to 1997. She is the only verified person to have lived past the age of 120.

lessons.name: Stack of Donuts
lessons.text1: The world record for tallest stack of donuts was about five feet tall and shaped like a pyramid. Computer software, an architect, and a structural engineer all contributed to the project. It was made up of 3,100 donuts.

lessons.name: World Records Game 1
lessons.text1: world record burp donut bubble building tower humans oldest loudest tallest largest

lessons.name: Fastest Clap
lessons.text1: Have you ever clapped so much that your hands started to hurt? A nine-year-old holds the record for the fastest clapping. He clapped his hands 1,080 times in a minute, which is about 18 claps per second!

lessons.name: Largest Pizza
lessons.text1: Have you ever baked a large pizza? The largest pizza ever made was 13,990 square feet. It was so large it had to be made in the Los Angeles Convention Center. Once everything was placed on the pizza, it was cooked in sections and donated to local food banks.

lessons.name: LEGO Train
lessons.text1: Are you ready for another world record involving LEGOs? The record for the most carriages in a toy train went to 14-year-old Alexander Blong from New Zealand. His LEGO train had 101 carriages. To win the record, his train also had to travel a minimum distance of 10 meters.

lessons.name: Ice Cream Scoops
lessons.text1: Have you ever struggled to keep two scoops of ice cream on your cone? Imagine balancing 125 scoops on a single cone! That is the current world record held by Dimitri Panciera from Italy, who managed to stack 125 scoops on a single cone.

lessons.name: Tallest Ice Cream
lessons.text1: Do you want to learn about another ice cream world record? The tallest ice cream cone ever made was 3.08 meters (or 10 feet and 1.26 inches) tall. It was created in Norway on July 26, 2015. The complete ice cream cone was made up of a wafer cone, chocolate lining, ice cream, and jam.

lessons.name: The Cake Boss
lessons.text1: Let's learn some world records about another tasty treat: cupcakes! How long does it take you to ice a cupcake? Buddy Valastro, also known as "The Cake Boss," set the record for icing 36 cupcakes in one minute on Live! with Kelly and Ryan in 2019.

lessons.name: How Many Cupcakes
lessons.text1: How many cupcakes can you eat in six minutes? The world record is currently 72 cupcakes. Pat "Deep Dish" Bertoletti ate 72 cupcakes in under six minutes at the Second Annual World Cupcake Eating Championship in 2012.

lessons.name: Cupcake Tower
lessons.text1: Not tired of learning about cupcake world records yet? Let's learn one more! The tallest tower of cupcakes was recorded in South Africa in 2017. It was 10.7 meters tall and made up of 6,370 cupcakes. That's a lot of cupcakes!

lessons.name: Socks
lessons.text1: Did you know there is even a world record for who can put on the most socks in 30 seconds? The current world record is 28 socks on one foot in 30 seconds. If you are up for the challenge, remember these guidelines: the socks must be store-bought, go over your ankle, and have no holes.

lessons.name: Around the World Introduction
lessons.text1: So many interesting places exist throughout the world. Here are some incredible facts about locations around the world that will have you astonished as you practice your typing skills!

lessons.name: Central Park
lessons.text1: Central Park in New York City offers an escape from the busy city life. It's also the most filmed location in the world!

lessons.name: Little Paris
lessons.text1: On the outskirts of Hangzhou, China lies "Little Paris," a luxury development featuring an Eiffel Tower replica (one-third the original's size), an Arc de Triomphe, and French-inspired boulevards and architecture.

lessons.name: CopenHill
lessons.text1: Denmark was ranked the cleanest country in 2021. It has charm, culture, and eco-innovation. CopenHill, a waste-to-energy plant with a rooftop ski slope, turns garbage into power and offers year-round skiing fun at the same time!

lessons.name: Oymyakon
lessons.text1: Oymyakon is a village in northeast Russia's Yakutia region. With temperatures as low as -70 degrees Celsius, it is known as The Pole of Cold. It's home to 500 people who hunt, fish, herd reindeer, and endure extreme conditions. Tourism draws adventurous visitors there!

lessons.name: Mongolia
lessons.text1: Mongolia, a landlocked nation between Russia and China, has the world's lowest population density. Its vast, dramatic landscapes, with mountains, plateaus, grasslands, and deserts, offer unparalleled solitude. If you need some alone time, this is the place!

lessons.name: Caves
lessons.text1: The Sacromonte and Guadix caves in Granada, Spain are home to communities preserving a 15th-century cave-dwelling lifestyle. These 2,000 stone-carved homes, once a refuge from persecution, now offer a way for residents to live off the land, continuing traditions from centuries past.

lessons.name: Ocean Atlas
lessons.text1: Beneath the crystal-clear water of the Bahamas lies "Ocean Atlas," the world's largest underwater sculpture. Weighing 60 tons and standing 18 feet tall, it was created by Jason deCaires Taylor, whose works often restore sea life to barren seabeds by attracting colorful marine ecosystems.

lessons.name: Liechtenstein
lessons.text1: Imagine walking across a whole country in hours. Liechtenstein is just 15 miles from north to south and 2.5 miles from east to west, making it possible to walk the entire country in less than a day. You'll need some sturdy hiking boots though, as you'll be walking in the steep inclines of the Alps.

lessons.name: Time Zones
lessons.text1: The top three countries with the most time zones are the United States, Russia, and France! The United States has 9 time zones, Russia spans 11 time zones, and France has a whopping 12 time zones!

lessons.name: Nazare
lessons.text1: Nazare, Portugal is home to Europe's largest submarine canyon. This area produces waves up to 100 feet tall, making it a hotspot for daredevil surfers. Just 1.5 hours from Lisbon, it's perfect for a thrilling day trip!

lessons.name: White Nights
lessons.text1: Between May and July, St. Petersburg, Russia experiences "White Nights," where the sky never fully darkens due to its high latitude near the Arctic Circle. Enjoy almost 24 hours of sunlight while exploring museums, gardens, and dining in during the festival.

lessons.name: Kathmandu
lessons.text1: Kathmandu, Nepal's capital and the gateway to Mount Everest, was once a lake. Fossils show that this lake existed 2.8 million years ago. Today, it's a stunning city of heritage sites, temples, and breathtaking mountain views. Visitors can even book flights over Mount Everest!

lessons.name: Orkney Islands
lessons.text1: The shortest commercial flight in the world is from Westray to Papa Westray in the Orkney Islands of Scotland. The flight usually lasts only 1 to 2 minutes and covers a distance of just 1.7 miles. It's operated by Scottish airline Loganair. Their fastest flight was 53 seconds!

lessons.name: Snake Island
lessons.text1: Just off the coast of southern Brazil lies one of the most dangerous places on Earth. It's called "Snake Island," and it is home to between 2,000 and 4,000 deadly golden lancehead vipers. These snakes have venom 3 to 5 times stronger than the mainland species. Brazil bans visitors except trained scientists.

lessons.name: Underwater Mail
lessons.text1: The world's deepest postbox is located near a fishing town in Susami Bay, Japan. It is 10 meters underwater and was installed to promote tourism. It allows divers to send postcards from underwater using waterproof postcards and oil-based paint markers to write their messages!

lessons.name: Countries
lessons.text1: There are no countries in the world whose names begin with the letter X. Letters that rarely appear at the beginning of country names are Q, Y, O, W, and Z. Can you think of countries starting with those letters? They include Qatar, Yemen, Oman, Wales, Zambia, and Zimbabwe!

lessons.name: Australia
lessons.text1: Did you know Australia is actually wider than the moon? While the moon's diameter is 3,475 kilometers, Australia's diameter is almost 4,000 kilometers! Despite its size, Australia is home to only 25 million people. Australia has roughly the same population as Texas, even though it's over five times larger!
